# What Feels Likely

*Availability, Affect, and Resemblance*

*Three useful cues become misleading when they silently replace value, frequency, or conditional probability*

::: {#chapter-09-start .chapter-epigraph}
> “People rely on a limited number of heuristic principles which reduce the complex tasks of assessing probabilities and predicting values to simpler judgmental operations.”
>
> — Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, [“Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases”](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124), 1974, p. 1124
:::

A product failure appears in your news feed, then in a colleague's message, and finally in the evening news. By the time someone asks whether the product is safe, an image of the failure comes immediately to mind. It feels alarming, and it resembles other disasters you remember.

You now seem to have several reasons for concern, enough perhaps to stop using the product or recommend that others do the same. But these impressions may all come from the same event. Repetition has made the evidence feel stronger without establishing how often failure occurs. Before acting, we need to distinguish what feels alarming from what the available evidence says about the risk.

::: {.callout-note .core-idea icon=false}
## Core Idea

Feelings, memorable examples, and resemblance can guide useful judgments. They become misleading when they substitute for the probability or comparison the decision requires. Trace each impression to its source, then ask what broader evidence would establish its weight.

:::

## Learning goals

- Distinguish affect, availability, and representativeness by the question each shortcut answers.
- Explain why vivid cases and coherent prototypes can hide denominators and base rates.
- Redesign one risk judgment so that feeling, story, and statistical evidence remain visible but separate.


## When value substitutes for evidence: affect answers first

Concern about a harmful outcome gives us a reason to investigate and a reason to care. It does not yet tell us how likely the outcome is. The difficulty begins when the feeling answers both questions at once.

The affect heuristic occurs when people use feelings of goodness or badness as a guide to judgment. If something feels good, people tend to judge its benefits as high and its risks as low. If something feels bad, people tend to judge its risks as high and its benefits as low (Slovic et al., 2002).

A feeling can summarize relevant experience or reveal something we care about. The problem arises when an overall impression supplies an answer to a different question, such as how often harm occurs.

Alhakami and Slovic (1994) found that perceived risks and perceived benefits of activities were often negatively related in people’s judgments, even though risks and benefits can both be high. Finucane and colleagues (2000) then manipulated information about technologies: presenting benefits more favorably could also lower judged risk, although the message had supplied no corresponding evidence about safety. The same feeling was answering two questions. [Chapter 6](06-valuation-how-options-become-worth-choosing.qmd#emotion-tells-the-mind-what-matters) separates what an outcome means to us from how likely it is.

The illustration below invites a first impression about two species.

![Which species receives your immediate concern? The comparison separates immediate appeal from ecological importance.](../figures/affect-panda-sea-star.png){#fig-affect-panda-sea-star fig-alt="An original editorial illustration places an appealing giant panda in bamboo beside an ochre sea star in a rich intertidal ecosystem, giving both subjects equal visual weight." width="88%"}

For a hypothetical exercise, suppose independent evidence showed that protecting the less immediately appealing species would prevent more ecosystem damage per unit of spending. How would you revise an initial allocation? The question separates visual appeal from the evidence needed to pursue a specified conservation goal.

For the product failure, concern may identify a consequence worth preventing. It cannot tell us the failure rate without knowing how many comparable products were used, under which conditions, and for how long. Record the concern, then estimate that rate separately.

The source of the feeling matters. Schwarz and Clore (1983) found that current mood influenced reported life satisfaction and that drawing attention to the weather could reduce this effect by making an incidental source salient. Different emotions also carry different appraisals: fear and anger are both negative, yet experiments have linked them to different perceptions of certainty, control, and risk (Lerner & Keltner, 2001). Ask: **Is this feeling information about the option, or information carried into it?**

## When recall substitutes for frequency: availability

![Affect and availability become biases when a feeling or memorable case silently substitutes for probability and evidence.](../figures/affect-availability.svg){#fig-affect-availability fig-alt="Affect and available examples converge on a substituted judgment, followed by a denominator and reference-class audit."}

If failures are common, we might expect to recall many of them. The reverse inference is less secure: examples can come to mind easily because the same failure has been repeatedly displayed. A risk judgment needs to separate frequency in the world from accessibility in memory.

The availability heuristic occurs when people judge frequency, probability, or importance by how easily examples come to mind (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973). If examples are easy to recall or imagine, the event feels common or likely. If examples are hard to recall, the event feels rare or unlikely.

Recall is useful when experience samples the relevant setting reasonably well. Repeated late deliveries can inform a judgment about a supplier, but a recent dramatic failure may be easier to remember than years of ordinary performance. Vividness, recency, repetition, and media coverage can all change retrieval without changing the underlying event rate.

Lichtenstein and colleagues (1978) found that people’s estimates of causes of death were related to availability and media coverage. Dramatic causes were often overestimated, while less dramatic but more common causes were underestimated. Combs and Slovic (1979) similarly showed that newspaper coverage was related to distorted frequency judgments. Events that receive more attention become mentally available.

Recalling more examples of a trait would seem to strengthen the judgment. Yet the effort of retrieving them can supply a competing signal. Schwarz and colleagues (1991) asked participants to recall either six or twelve examples of assertive behavior. People who had to recall twelve examples often rated themselves as less assertive than those who recalled six, because retrieving twelve examples was difficult. The experience of difficulty became information. People did not simply count examples; they used ease of retrieval as a cue.

A team responding to a recent crisis should therefore ask whether the event revealed a new failure mechanism, changed an estimated frequency, or merely became easier to recall. These possibilities call for different responses. A broader record of comparable opportunities can help the team learn from the event without organizing every future decision around it.

## When category fit substitutes for probability: resemblance

![A category resemblance can suggest a hypothesis; updating its probability requires the prior and evidence that distinguishes competing explanations.](../figures/prototype-probability.svg){#fig-prototype-probability fig-alt="Two paths are contrasted. Resemblance produces a quick impression; prior probability and diagnostic evidence contribute independently to an updated probability."}

A familiar pattern helps us recognize what might be happening. But a convincing match can overshadow a more common explanation that looks less distinctive. For hiring, diagnosis, or investment, the cost is confusing a recognizable story with a well-supported forecast.

The **representativeness heuristic** judges a case by how closely it resembles a prototype or coherent story (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). A confident speaker looks like a leader. A quiet reader sounds like a librarian. A founder in a hoodie with an ambitious vision resembles a familiar story of technology success. Similarity can contain evidence, but probability also depends on how common the category is and how diagnostically the observed feature distinguishes it from alternatives.

The Linda problem reveals the substitution. Participants read about a bright, outspoken person concerned with discrimination and social justice. Many judge “Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement” more likely than “Linda is a bank teller” because the richer description fits better. Yet an event joined with an additional condition cannot be more probable than the event alone (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). Narrative fit answered “Which description resembles Linda?” while the target asked “Which event includes more possible cases?”

Hiring creates the same risk without a puzzle. A committee may treat confidence, polish, an elite degree, or conversational ease as signs of future performance because these features fit its image of talent. The right correction is not to ban resemblance; it is to specify the relevant reference class and test which observed features predict the defined job outcome. A prototype is a hypothesis about predictive features, not a competence measure.

Brief impressions can nevertheless predict how people respond to a prototype. Todorov et al. (2005) found that competence impressions formed from photographs of unfamiliar political candidates predicted election winners above chance.[^ch09-face-prediction] The hiring lesson is the same: a first impression can predict a chooser's reaction without measuring the job-relevant quality the chooser believes it sees.

[Chapter 14](14-base-rates-conditional-probability-and-bayesian-updating.qmd#worked-update-the-same-screen-in-two-applicant-pools) turns this hiring problem into a numerical comparison. At this stage, use three questions: **How common is the category? How diagnostic is the resemblance? What alternative category could produce the same features?** A good match to a story is not the same as a high conditional probability.

## When correlated cues look like independent evidence

Affect, availability, and resemblance often point in the same direction, which makes their conclusion feel multiply supported. A vivid case is easy to retrieve, emotionally charged, and representative of a familiar danger story. The three experiences can look like three pieces of evidence even when they come from one exposure.

Return to the product failure in the opening. Three reports and three psychological responses can all trace back to one incident. Before counting them as converging evidence, establish whether they add an observation or repeat one.

The same problem appears in hiring. One charismatic candidate reminds committee members of a successful former colleague. That remembered example becomes available; similarity activates a prototype; positive affect spills into forecasts of competence. The committee may say that “all the signals point the same way,” even though the signals are correlated outputs of one first impression.

The corrective is an **independence audit**. List each reason for the judgment, then trace its source. Did two reasons arise from the same anecdote? Did the feeling arise because the case was vivid? Did the prototype come from a success story selected after the outcome? Independent work samples, base rates, and criterion-specific ratings add genuinely new information. Rephrasing the same impression does not.

[Chapter 13](13-accessibility-familiarity-and-ease.qmd#repetition-can-become-liking-and-truth) explains why repetition can nevertheless increase a claim's apparent credibility. The source trail tells us whether the added confidence has earned any new support.

This is why the book treats mechanisms before labels. Naming three heuristics can create the illusion of three causes. A causal map asks whether one upstream cue generated all three.

## One risk, three shortcuts

Suppose a board must decide whether to suspend employee travel after a vivid aviation accident. Protecting employees is the objective, but a suspension must also be compared with the risks and costs of the available alternatives. Affect supplies dread and a protective impulse. Availability makes images of the accident easy to retrieve. Resemblance encourages the board to treat another flight as “the same kind of danger.” None of those responses is meaningless: the event may reveal a new hazard, and employee concern has value. But the target decision also requires exposure, a time window, relevant base rates, changes in the underlying process, and comparison with the risks created by alternative travel.

The disciplined response keeps all three layers. First, name the feeling and the value it protects. Second, record the cases that memory produced and why they are retrievable. Third, state the prototype and the causal features that make the current case comparable. Only then find a denominator and reference class. The goal is not to silence a vivid case; it is to learn what it can and cannot represent.

## From an impression to a distribution

Begin by preserving the impression, then identify the target question and the comparison it needs. “Ten failures” requires a denominator and time window; “one per million operations” requires checking whether those operations are comparable in exposure and severity. A reference class is a substantive choice about which cases belong together.

Finally, ask whether the vivid case reveals something the broader record misses. One near miss cannot estimate an accident rate, but it can reveal a new failure pathway. Intuition can suggest a hypothesis; evidence must then establish how much weight it deserves.

| Shortcut | Useful when | Misleads when | Corrective |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Affect | Feeling summarizes relevant, repeated experience. | Mood or identity spills into an unrelated forecast. | Name the feeling, then estimate probability separately. |
| Availability | Memory samples the environment fairly. | News, vividness, recency, or repetition distort retrieval. | Find the denominator and a representative reference class. |
| Resemblance | The prototype contains features validated for the target prediction. | Surface fit substitutes for prevalence or diagnosticity. | Add the base rate and ask what alternatives produce the same features. |
| Personal example | The case is diagnostically similar. | One case substitutes for a distribution. | Ask how often the pattern occurs across comparable cases. |
: When affect, availability, and resemblance help or mislead {#tbl-10-1}

## Practice Lab

Choose a professional risk that currently feels unusually large or small. Produce a one-page **story-to-statistics brief** containing: the immediate feeling and its source; the first three cases recalled and why they are memorable; the prototype being matched; the relevant denominator and time window; the base rate; and one feature that would make this case diagnostically different. End with a revised probability range and a separate statement of how bad the outcome would be.

## Take it forward

Return to the product failure that appeared in three places. Find out whether the reports describe one event or independent incidents, and whether the conditions match the product you might use. Concern can motivate that inquiry without determining its answer.

[^ch09-face-prediction]: The study measured election outcomes rather than governing competence. Candidate and photograph selection, exposure, stereotypes, and other correlated cues could contribute to the relationship (Todorov et al., 2005).
